archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (still below average)
archetype.definition: A team whose point differential and efficiency say it is a mid-pack-minus side rather than a three-win one, held down by close losses, sacks and soft coverage, but not good enough to make the gap matter for a playoff push.

report.headline: Better than 3-8, still not good: an average offense undone by leaky coverage
report.take:
The Jets are 3-8, but the record undersells them a little. A -57 point differential implies 4.7 wins, and they have won just 0.167 of their one-score games, 28th in the league. More telling is the comparison with last year. In 2025 they were dead last in net EPA at -0.271 with the 29th-ranked offense. This season they sit 23rd in net EPA and 17th on offense, with Geno Smith starting all eleven games. That is a real rise from the floor to below average, and the losses have mostly been competitive ones rather than blowouts.

The offense stays on schedule better than its scoring suggests. Its success rate ranks 9th, and it has given the ball away only 9 times. Where it bleeds is in the drive-killers. Smith has been sacked 33 times, a sack rate that ranks 26th. Short-yardage conversion is 31st. The team has also given away 643 yards in penalties, including 156 in a three-point loss to Green Bay. The defense mirrors that shape. The pass rush gets home: the sack rate is 5th and they have 29 sacks. Tackling is sound, with the missed-tackle rate 5th. The coverage behind it leaks, though. Pass EPA allowed is 30th and short-pass EPA allowed is 29th, and second receivers and tight ends have found room underneath.

The numbers hide two things. First, the record is not a turnover story. The Jets are +3 in turnover margin. The losing has come from close games slipping away: Green Bay and Miami by three, Las Vegas by five. Second, the run defense reads two ways. One cut ranks rush EPA allowed 10th. The play-by-play cut ranks it 30th, with explosive runs allowed 29th. The box scores side with the second view: Chicago ran for 232, Buffalo for 201 and Miami for 156 in the first meeting.

Where this heads is roughly where the underlying numbers point. They should win a couple of the soft spots left, at Miami and at Arizona, and lose most of the games against Denver, Minnesota and Buffalo. That adds up to a five- or six-win team that looks more like a foundation than last year's. It does not look like a team close to contention.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: The Jets don't pressure at an elite rate, but when they get there they get the quarterback down. They had 8 sacks against Cleveland and 6 at the Chargers. A sack rate this high on middling pressure partly reflects coverage holding early on some snaps, so expect some regression. It is still a genuine weapon against shaky protection.

strengths.title: Offense stays on schedule, protects ball
strengths.body: A 9th-ranked success rate and only 9 giveaways in eleven games describe an offense that grinds out positive plays and doesn't beat itself with turnovers. It is a sharp turnaround from 2025, when the offense ranked 29th in EPA and the turnover margin was last. With the same quarterback starting every week, this looks durable.

strengths.title: Sure tackling limits damage
strengths.body: A 5th-ranked missed-tackle rate is why the defense ranks 13th in explosive passes allowed despite the poor overall coverage numbers. Completions underneath are getting through, but they rarely turn into chunk plays. Tackling tends to be a stable trait.

concerns.title: Coverage leaks underneath
concerns.body: Pass EPA allowed ranks 30th, and the damage is short. Short-pass EPA allowed is 29th, and tight ends and second receivers gain efficiently against them. This is a real structural flaw, not bad luck. It is also why third downs (23rd) and red-zone trips (22nd) go against them.

concerns.title: Sacks and short yardage stall drives
concerns.body: The offense moves the ball, but drives die on sacks and failed short-yardage tries. The sack rate allowed ranks 26th and short-yardage conversion 31st. That combination turns a 9th-ranked success rate into a 25th-ranked scoring offense. The line's 25th-ranked stuff rate suggests the short-yardage problem lives up front.

concerns.title: Explosive runs against them
concerns.body: Depending on the cut, the run defense looks fine or bad. The explosive-run rate (29th) and the game log show the bad version too often: 232 yards to Chicago, 201 to Buffalo. Run-heavy opponents can lean on this.

trend.note: They opened 2-3 in mostly tight games, dropped five straight from Week 6 to Week 10, then won 27-24 at the Chargers behind 6 sacks and their best passing game of the year. The passing EPA swings wildly from week to week: deeply negative at Kansas City and against Buffalo, strongly positive against Miami, Las Vegas and the Chargers.

nextGame.headline: Favored in Miami against the league's worst defense by EPA
nextGame.body:
The Jets go to 1-9 Miami as 3.5-point favorites, with a total of 40.5 and a -214 moneyline. They lost the first meeting 25-28 at home despite throwing well. On paper this is their best matchup left. Miami ranks last in defensive EPA, 31st in pass EPA allowed and 26th on deep passes, and has only 12 sacks. That should give Smith the clean pockets he rarely gets. The danger is stylistic. Miami runs far more than expected (pass rate over expected 31st), and its line creates yards before contact (3rd). That points straight at the Jets' habit of allowing explosive runs.

Availability tilts toward New York. Malik Willis is on injured reserve, so Kyle McCord makes his third start for an offense that already ranked 26th in EPA. Miami's punter Bradley Pinion is out, and starting corner JuJu Brents is questionable with a shoulder injury. On the Jets' side, receivers Isaiah Williams and Omar Cooper Jr. were listed out after the Chargers game. Their return estimate is this week but not confirmed, which could leave Garrett Wilson and the tight ends to carry the passing game. DT David Onyemata (IR) and LB Trevin Wallace remain sidelined.

waysToWin.title: Throw on a broken pass defense
waysToWin.body: Miami allows the second-worst pass EPA in the league and struggles badly on deep throws. It also generates little pass rush, which takes away the Jets' biggest offensive leak, sacks. With Brents questionable, Smith should have room to push the ball the way he did in the first meeting.

waysToWin.title: Tight ends up the seam
waysToWin.body: Miami ranks last in EPA allowed to tight ends and sees an above-average share of targets go to the position. With two receivers possibly out, feeding Kenyon Sadiq and Mason Taylor is the natural adjustment and the softest spot in the opponent's coverage.

waysToWin.title: Get after a backup quarterback
waysToWin.body: McCord plays behind a line with the 30th-ranked sack rate allowed, and the Jets finish pressure as well as almost anyone. If they force Miami off its run script, drive-ending sacks and Miami's weak special teams, now without its punter, should hand the Jets a field-position edge.

waysToLose.title: Gashed on the ground again
waysToLose.body: Miami ran for 156 yards in the first meeting and is one of the most run-heavy teams in football. Its line creates space before contact. If the Jets' explosive-run problem shows up, Miami can shorten the game, protect McCord and keep it inside a field goal.

waysToLose.title: Close-game habits resurface
waysToLose.body: A low total and a short spread point to another one-score game, and the Jets have lost almost all of those. Penalties have been a recurring drive-killer and, in Week 2, a game-changer. Their failures in short yardage can turn red-zone trips into field goals in a game where points will be scarce.

waysToLose.title: Thin receiver room stalls
waysToLose.body: If Williams and Cooper sit, Wilson becomes the obvious target. Miami's defense has held opposing top receivers well under their usual output. A bracketed Wilson plus the usual sacks could produce one of the flat passing days the Jets had against Kansas City and Buffalo.

nextGame.watch: Miami's early-down runs: if the Jets' front holds them under 4 yards a carry and forces McCord into passing downs, their pass rush takes over; if not, it is another three-point game.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying profile is that of a team somewhat better than 3-8. The point differential implies more than four wins, and the close-game record should even out somewhat. But the defense's coverage problems and the offense's sack and short-yardage issues are structural, not noise, so don't expect a surge. The remaining schedule splits cleanly. Miami and Arizona are winnable, the latter with the 31st-ranked defense by EPA. New England is a coin flip at home. Denver, Minnesota's top-ranked defense and Buffalo on the road are likely losses.

What's sustainable: ball security, an efficient early-down offense and a finishing pass rush. What may regress: the high sack rate on average pressure, and the boom weeks in passing EPA. Realistically this ends at five or six wins. The step up from 2025 is real, but the defense needs coverage help before the record follows the efficiency.
swingFactors: Health of the receiver room behind Garrett Wilson

confidence.note: Eleven games with the same starting quarterback is a solid sample, but the run-defense metrics conflict and the close-game results are noisy.
